extracted.intended_audience: 18th-century educated public, builders/householders, and natural philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and observational guidance for securing buildings and persons from lightning, plus instructions for an electrical kite experiment and explanations of meteorological phenomena (whirlwinds, water-spouts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of lightning and electricity
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments made in electricity first gave philosophers a suspicion that the matter of lightning was the same with the electric matter... experiments... have since proved this suspicion to be perfectly well founded; and that, whatever properties we find in electricity, are also the properties of lightning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat lightning as the same subtile electric fluid observed in laboratory experiments; methods and inferences from electrical experiments apply to lightning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the electric fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: This matter of lightning or of electricity is an extreme subtile fluid, penetrating other bodies, and subsisting in them, equally diffused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptualize electricity as a penetrative fluid that distributes itself among bodies according to relative quantities and available conductors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge equalization and observable phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is a greater proportion of this fluid in one body than in another, the body which has most will communicate to that which has least... If the communication be through the air without any conductor, a bright light is seen between the bodies, and a sound is heard (electric spark / lightning and thunder). If the communication of this fluid is by a conductor, it may be without either light or sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect sparks/lightning and thunder for air discharges; expect silent transfer when a continuous conductor connects charged bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conductors and non-conductors (materials guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: All metals and water are good conductors. Other bodies may become conductors by having some quantity of water in them... Glass, wax, silk, wool, hair, feathers, and even wood, perfectly dry, are non-conductors: that is, they resist instead of facilitating the passage of this subtile fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing risk or constructing protective paths for electric discharge, prefer metals and water as conductors; avoid relying on wood or dry organic materials as conductors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior when multiple conductors present
rubrics_metrics.description: When this fluid has an opportunity of passing through two conductors, one good and sufficient, as of metal, the other not so good, it passes in the best, and will follow it in any direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the presence of a clearly superior continuous conductor (metal rod to earth) so the discharge will follow it rather than less effective conductors embedded in structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Striking distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance at which a body charged with this fluid will discharge itself suddenly, striking through the air into another body that is not charged or not so highly charged, is different according to the quantity of the fluid, the dimensions and form of the bodies themselves, and the state of the air between them. This distance... is called the striking distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that risk of discharge depends on charge quantity, object geometry, and air conditions; elevation of conductors changes whether objects fall within striking distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of tall objects as partial conductors
rubrics_metrics.description: Tall trees and lofty buildings, as the towers and spires of churches, become sometimes conductors between the clouds and the earth; but, not being good ones, that is, not conveying the fluid freely, they are often damaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on tall structures alone for safety; if they are not good conductors (continuous metal paths to earth) they attract strikes and suffer damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buildings with metal roofs and metal downspouts are protected
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings that have their roofs covered with lead or other metal, the spouts of metal continued from the roof into the ground to carry off the water, are never hurt by lightning as, whenever it falls on such a building, it passes in the metals and not in the walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity of metal from roof to ground offers reliable protection—ensure metal roofing and metal conductors are continuous into earth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal partial conductors can cause internal damage
rubrics_metrics.description: When other buildings happen to be within the striking distance... the fluid passes in the walls... quitting the walls only when it can find better conductors near them, as metal rods, bolts, and hinges of windows or doors, gilding on wainscot or frames of pictures, the silvering on the backs of looking-glasses, the wires for bells, and the bodies of animals, as containing watery fluids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and, if possible, mitigate or isolate internal metallic fixtures and conductive decorations that provide paths for lightning into interior structures and occupants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and placement of an external iron lightning rod
rubrics_metrics.description: An iron rod being placed on the outside of a building, from the highest part continued down into the moist earth in any direction... will receive the lightning at the upper end, attracting it so as to prevent its striking any other part, and affording it a good conveyance into the earth, will prevent its damaging any part of the building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install a continuous iron rod from the highest exterior point straight into moist earth to intercept strikes and convey the current safely away from building fabric and occupants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended rod elevation, shape and finishing
rubrics_metrics.description: We elevate the upper end of the rod six or eight feet above the highest part of the building, tapering it gradually to a fine sharp point, which is gilt to prevent its rusting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the rod extend several feet above the roofline, taper to a sharp point (to draw charge), and gild or otherwise protect the tip from corrosion to maintain efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended rod grounding details
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower end of the rod should enter the earth so deep as to come at the moist part, perhaps two or three feet; and if bent when under the surface so as to go in a horizontal line six or eight feet from the wall, and then bent again downward three or four feet, it will prevent damage to any of the stones of the foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the rod's buried end reaches damp soil; routing it horizontally beneath the footing before descending prevents damaging currents through foundation stones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rod diameter and conductor sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A small quantity of metal is found able to conduct a great quantity of this fluid. A wire no bigger than a goosequill has been known to conduct (with safety to the building as far as the wire was continued) a quantity of lightning that did prodigious damage both above and below it; and probably larger rods are not necessary, though it is common in America to make them of half an inch, some of three quarters or an inch diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even thin metal conductors can safely carry large discharges if continuous to earth; common practice uses rods from ~1/2 to 1 inch diameter but continuity and grounding matter more than sheer mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fastening rods to structure with iron staples
rubrics_metrics.description: The rod may be fastened to the wall, chimney &c., with staples of iron. The lightning will not leave the rod (a good conductor) through those staples. It would rather, if any were in the walls, pass out of it into the rod, to get more readily by that conductor into the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iron staples or fastenings to attach rods—the discharge prefers the continuous rod and will not divert destructively through those staples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple rods for very large buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: If the building be very large and extensive, two or more rods may be placed at different parts, for greater security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple interceptors spaced across large roofs to reduce risk from strikes at different locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointed rods can prevent strokes by drawing charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Long sharp points communicating with the earth, and presented to such parts of clouds, drawing silently from them the fluid they are charged with, they are then attracted to the cloud, and may leave the distance so great as to be beyond the reach of striking... Thus the pointed rod either prevents the stroke from the cloud, or, if a stroke is made, conducts it to the earth with safety to the building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharp elevated points can quietly dissipate charge from nearby cloud fragments, potentially preventing strikes; this is an explicit rationale for pointed/gilded rod tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk from suspended partial cloud conductors
rubrics_metrics.description: Small ragged parts of clouds, suspended in the air between the great body of clouds and the earth... often serve as partial conductors for the lightning, which proceeds from one of them to another, and by their help comes within the striking distance to the earth or a building. It therefore strikes through those conductors a building that would otherwise be out of the striking distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for transient suspended cloud fragments when assessing strike risk—these can extend the effective reach of a discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe behavior inside an unprotected house during thunder
rubrics_metrics.description: A person apprehensive of danger from lightning... will do well to avoid sitting near the chimney, near a looking-glass, or any gilt pictures or wainscot; the safest place is the middle of the room (so it be not under a metal lustre suspended by a chain), sitting on one chair and laying the feet up in another. It is still safer to bring two or three mattresses or beds into the middle of the room, and, folding them up double, place the chair upon them... a hammock or swinging bed, suspended by silk cords equally distant from the walls on every side, and from the ceiling and floor above and below, affords the safest situation a person can have in any room whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When indoors without a protective rod system, avoid proximity to interior metallic conductors or gilded surfaces; center yourself away from walls and metal fixtures; insulating bedding or a silk-suspended hammock reduces conduction paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kite experiment construction and precautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a small cross of two light strips of cedar... tie the corners of the handkerchief... fix a very sharp-pointed wire to the top of the upright stick rising a foot or more above the wood. To the end of the twine next the hand is to be tied a silk riband, and where the silk and twine join, a key may be fastened. This kite is to be raised when a thunder-gust appears to be coming on, and the person who holds the string must stand within a door or window, or under some cover, so that the silk riband may not be wet; and care must be taken that the twine does not touch the frame of the door or window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct kite of silk sailcloth on cedar cross with pointed metal spike; attach key at silk–twine junction; operator must remain sheltered so the silk stays dry and avoid contact between twine and frames to prevent unintended conductive paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kite experiment observation and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as any of the thunder-clouds come over the kite, the pointed wire will draw the electric fire from them... the loose filaments of the twine will stand out every way, and be attracted by an approaching finger. And when the rain has wetted the kite and twine... you will find it stream out plentifully from the key on the approach of your knuckle. At this key the vial may be charged; and from electric fire thus obtained, spirits may be kindled, and all the other electric experiments be performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect visual signs of electrification (filaments standing out) and, once wet, streaming from the key; the arrangement can be used as a source of electric charge comparable to rubbed glass globes for experiments—take shelter and avoid grounding yourself directly to the twine when collecting charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning damage when conductor insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conductor be good and of sufficient bigness, the fluid passes through it without hurting it. If otherwise, it is damaged or destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure conductor continuity and sufficient cross-section for the intended installation; inadequate conductors can be damaged and can permit destructive branching through surrounding materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism and causes of whirlwinds and water-spouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whirlwinds generally arise after calms and great heats... the rising will begin precisely in that column that happens to be the lightest or most rarefied; and the warm air will flow horizontally from all points to this column, where the several currents meeting, and joining to rise, a whirl is naturally formed... they ascend by a spiral motion... the vacuum round the axis of the whirl should be greatest near the earth or sea, and be gradually diminished as it approaches the region of the clouds...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model whirlwinds/water-spouts as arising from localized rising columns of heated air with converging horizontal inflows producing spiral ascent and an axial rarefaction/vacuum; anticipate strongest effects near the surface and possible columns of water lifted up to ~30 feet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions and observed effects of whirlwinds/water-spouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Water-spouts have, also, a progressive motion... Whirlwinds and spouts are not always, though most commonly, in the daytime... The augmentation of the cloud... during a spout seems to show an ascent rather than a descent... effects: stripping off the roofs, blowing away chimneys, breaking doors and windows, forcing up the floors, and unpaving the rooms... carry up into the air tiles, stones, and animals themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect whirlwinds after prolonged heating/calm conditions, with the capacity to lift and scatter heavy debris; when assessing risk or interpreting reports, look for progressive motion, cloud augmentation, and destructive lifting consistent with an ascending spiral.
